hints: Look carefully at the two curves and the labels A, B, C, D. Which curve is for high carbon dioxide, and do A and B show high or low oxygen saturation?
Remember when chloride ions move into the red blood cell. It happens during the chloride shift when lots of carbon dioxide is being carried as hydrogencarbonate ions.
walkthrough:
**Recall why chloride enters the red cell**

Think of respiring tissues releasing lots of carbon dioxide. Inside the red cell, carbon dioxide forms hydrogen ions and hydrogencarbonate ions.

To keep charge balanced as hydrogencarbonate leaves the cell, chloride ions move in:
$$HCO_3^- \text{ out} \rightarrow Cl^- \text{ in}$$

**Link this to oxygen and carbon dioxide conditions**

Most chloride inside the cell means most carbon dioxide is being transported. That happens where $pCO_2$ is high.

It also happens where haemoglobin is unloading oxygen, so $pO_2$ is low and percentage saturation is low. This is the Bohr shift to the right.

**Read positions A, B, C and D**

A and B are both at low $pO_2$ and low saturation, but A is on the low $pCO_2$ curve and B is on the high $pCO_2$ curve.

C and D are both at high $pO_2$ and high saturation, like in the lungs where carbon dioxide is released and chloride leaves the cell. So B fits best.

options.A: Low saturation is correct for unloading, but this is the low carbon dioxide curve, so little hydrogencarbonate is made and little chloride enters.
options.B: High carbon dioxide curve plus low oxygen saturation means active unloading in respiring tissues, maximum chloride shift into the cell.
options.C: High saturation on the low carbon dioxide curve is like the lungs, where haemoglobin loads oxygen and chloride ions leave the cell.
options.D: Although on the high carbon dioxide curve, high saturation at high pO2 means loading oxygen, the reverse of the chloride shift conditions.
